title: Generative AI at Work: Save Hours Every Week
subtitle: Use a chat assistant to write, summarise, research, plan and work in spreadsheets faster, while checking its work and keeping your organisation's data safe.
skills: Safe use of AI at work
tools: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
outcomes: Write clear prompts that give a chat assistant the context, task, audience and format it needs
Draft, edit and adapt emails and documents with AI while keeping the facts and your own voice
Summarise documents and research topics with AI, and check its claims against sources
Get, understand and test spreadsheet formulas with an assistant's help
Build a personal prompt library that saves measurable time, within your organisation's privacy rules
prerequisites: None: you only need to be comfortable with email, documents and a little spreadsheet work. You need access to a chat assistant such as Claude (a free plan is enough for the labs) and a spreadsheet program. If your organisation has an AI policy or a list of approved tools, have it to hand.
description: A chat assistant can take hours of routine work off your week, but only if you know how to ask, what to check and what never to paste in. This course shows you, task by task. You'll learn how chat assistants work and why they sometimes make things up, write prompts that get a useful answer first time, and keep personal and confidential data safe. Then you'll put the assistant to work: drafting and editing emails and documents in your own voice, summarising long documents and researching topics with every claim checked, writing and testing spreadsheet formulas, turning meetings into action lists and planning your week. Every module has a hands-on lab with sample material, and you'll finish by building your own prompt library and measuring the time it saves you.

modules.title: Getting good answers, safely
modules.summary: How chat assistants work and why they get things wrong, the parts of a prompt that matter, and the privacy rules to follow before you paste anything in.

lessons.title: How chat assistants work, and where they go wrong
objectives: Explain how a chat assistant produces its answers
Identify the tasks assistants are good at and the ones that need care
key_points: A chat assistant runs on a large language model, which writes a reply by predicting likely next words from patterns in huge amounts of text, so its answers sound fluent whether or not they're right.
Assistants can make things up, which is called hallucination: invented facts, figures, quotes and references, so anything that matters needs checking.
A model's built-in knowledge stops at its training cutoff; some assistants can search the web or read files you upload, and then answer from those sources, which you can check.
Within a conversation the assistant uses what has been said so far; whether it remembers anything between conversations depends on the product and on settings such as memory.

Assistants are strong at drafting, rewriting, summarising, explaining, brainstorming and turning messy notes into structure; they need more care with exact facts, recent events and judgements that depend on your organisation.

lessons.title: Prompts that work
objectives: Write prompts with context, task, audience, format and constraints
Improve an answer with specific follow-up requests
key_points: A good prompt gives context (your role and the situation), the task, the audience, the format you want and any constraints, such as length, tone or what to leave out.
An example of what good looks like, such as a previous email you liked, helps the assistant match your style better than adjectives alone.
Asking the assistant to ask you questions before it starts helps with complex tasks, or when you're not sure which details matter.
Treat the first answer as a draft and follow up with specific changes, such as 'shorter, warmer and with the deadline first', rather than starting again.
Keep the material to work on, such as text to edit or notes to summarise, clearly apart from your instructions, for example under a heading or between quotation marks.

walkthrough.title: From a vague prompt to a useful one

steps.do: Start a new conversation and try a vague prompt.
steps.code: Write an email about the team meeting.
steps.see: A generic email full of placeholders such as [date] and [time], because the assistant had nothing to go on.

steps.do: Start again with context, task, audience, format and constraints.
steps.code:
I lead a team of eight in a customer-support department.
Task: write an email moving our weekly team meeting from Monday 9:00 to Tuesday 14:00, starting next week, because Monday mornings are our busiest time.
Audience: my team, who are used to the old time.
Format: a subject line and no more than 80 words.
Tone: friendly and brief. Ask them to tell me by Friday if the new time clashes with anything.
steps.see: A short, specific email with a subject line, the new time, the reason and the Friday deadline.

steps.do: Follow up with a specific change instead of rewriting the prompt.
steps.code: Good. Put the new time in the first sentence and make the subject line say what changed.

steps.do: For a bigger task, ask the assistant to ask first.
steps.code: I need to write a one-page proposal for a new staff rota. Before you write anything, ask me up to five questions about what you need to know.
steps.see: Questions about the team, the problem with the current rota, constraints and who must approve it.

lessons.title: What's safe to share: privacy and company policies
objectives: Decide what information may and may not go into a chat assistant
Find and follow your organisation's rules on AI use
key_points: Treat anything you type or upload into a chat assistant as leaving your organisation, unless your organisation has approved that tool for that kind of information.
Don't paste personal data about customers or colleagues, confidential business information, passwords or access keys into a tool your organisation hasn't approved for them.

Consumer and business plans of the same assistant can handle data differently, for example in whether conversations may be used to train models and how long they're kept; check the settings and the terms.
Many organisations have an AI policy that lists approved tools, says what data may go into them and when AI use must be disclosed; follow it, and ask when it's unclear.
Remove or replace identifying details before asking for help, such as writing 'Customer A' instead of a name, and describe a spreadsheet's columns rather than pasting its data.
You remain responsible for what you send or publish, including checking AI output for accuracy, confidentiality and fairness.

lab.title: Before and after: improve a prompt
lab.goal: Take a real task from your work, see what a vague prompt gives you, then rewrite the prompt so the first answer is close to usable.
setup: A chat assistant such as Claude, in a plan your organisation allows for work
A writing task from your work that contains no personal or confidential information, such as a team update or a notice

steps.do: Choose the task. If it involves people or confidential details, replace them with placeholders such as Customer A or [amount] before you start.
Write the shortest prompt you'd naturally type for it, run it, and copy the prompt and the answer under the heading Before prompt.
Rewrite the prompt with labelled parts: Context, Task, Audience, Format and Constraints. Add an example of the style you want if you have one.
Start a new conversation, run the new prompt, and copy it and the answer under the heading After prompt.
Ask one specific follow-up that improves the answer, and copy it with the result.
In a new conversation, ask the assistant to ask you questions before it writes, for a bigger version of the same task. Copy its questions under the heading Questions it asked.
Under the heading What changed, write two or three sentences comparing the before and after answers, and how long each would take to make usable.

checks.text: The before prompt and its answer are included.
The improved prompt has context, task, audience, format and constraints, and its answer is included.
A specific follow-up request improves the answer.
The assistant was asked to ask questions first, and its questions are included.
The comparison says what improved, and no personal or confidential details appear anywhere.

lab.submit: Paste your Before prompt and After prompt sections (prompts and answers), your follow-up, the Questions it asked section and your What changed notes.
hints: If the after answer still has gaps, look for the fact the assistant had to guess and add it to the prompt.
Label your follow-up with the word follow-up so it's easy to find.

modules.title: Writing and editing
modules.summary: Draft emails and documents from your facts, edit for tone and plain language, adapt one message for several audiences, and check every draft before it goes out.

lessons.title: Drafting emails and documents
objectives: Give an assistant what it needs to draft a message that does its job
Plan longer documents with an outline before drafting
key_points: Give the assistant the purpose, the reader, the key facts and the outcome you want, such as 'confirm the new date and ask for a reply by Friday', so the draft does its job.
For longer documents, ask for an outline first, with headings and a line under each, and agree it before asking for the full text.
Supply the facts yourself rather than letting the assistant fill gaps: when details are missing, it may invent plausible ones, such as dates, names or figures.
Keep your own voice by giving a sample of your writing or a few rules, such as 'short sentences, no jargon, sign off with my first name'.
Where the relationship matters most, such as condolences or difficult feedback, consider writing the message yourself and using the assistant only to review it.

lessons.title: Editing, tone and plain language
objectives: Use an assistant to edit for clarity, length and tone
Adapt one message for different audiences without changing what it says
key_points: Assistants are good editors: ask them to shorten, simplify, restructure, fix grammar or change the tone, and say what must stay unchanged.
Ask for a list of the changes, or for suggestions instead of a rewrite, so you can see each edit and choose which to keep.
Plain language means short sentences, everyday words, active verbs and the main point first; it helps every reader, including people reading in a second language.
Adapting one message for different audiences, such as staff, customers and managers, is quick with an assistant, but check each version still says the same thing.
Edits can change meaning, so compare the facts, commitments and conditions in the new version with the original before you use it.

walkthrough.title: Edit with suggestions you can choose from

steps.do: Paste a paragraph you've written, with instructions kept apart from it.
steps.code:
Suggest edits to make the paragraph below clearer and shorter for busy managers. Don't rewrite it: list each suggestion with the original words and your replacement, and the reason. Don't change any numbers or dates.

Paragraph:
"""
[paste your paragraph here]
"""
steps.see: A numbered list of suggested changes, each with a reason.

steps.do: Accept some suggestions and reject others, then ask for the edited version.
steps.code: Apply suggestions 1, 3 and 4 only, and show the result.

steps.do: Ask for a version for a different audience.
steps.code: Now write a version of the same message for customers: friendlier, no internal jargon, and under 60 words. Keep every date and number the same.

steps.do: Compare the facts in each version with your original, line by line, before using either.

lessons.title: Checking what it wrote, and owning it
objectives: Check an AI-drafted message before it goes out
Explain why responsibility stays with the sender
key_points: Before sending anything drafted with AI, check every fact, number, date, name and promise against your sources.
Watch for confident filler: claims that sound plausible but weren't in your notes, such as an invented policy or a deadline nobody agreed.
Check the tone for the reader and the relationship: a polished but generic message can come across as cold or insincere.
Follow your organisation's rules on disclosing AI use, and never present work as checked if you haven't checked it.
You're responsible for what you send, so the time saved should come from faster drafting, not from skipping the review.

lab.title: Rewrite a messy announcement for two audiences
lab.goal: Turn a rushed draft into a clear staff announcement and a short team-chat message, keeping every fact exactly right.
setup: A chat assistant such as Claude
Download rough_announcement.txt: a fictional, rushed draft about a new room-booking system

steps.do: Read rough_announcement.txt and list its facts yourself first: the dates, times, room, deadline and contact address. Note anything that doesn't belong in the message.
Ask the assistant for a staff announcement, giving it the draft as material to work on.
steps.code:
Rewrite the draft below as a clear announcement to all staff.
Format: a subject line starting Subject:, then no more than 150 words, with the most important change first and the dates easy to find.
Keep every fact, date, time and address exactly as in the draft. Leave out anything that isn't about room booking.

Draft:
"""
[paste rough_announcement.txt here]
"""

steps.do: Ask for a team-chat version of no more than 50 words that points people to the full announcement. Copy it under the heading Chat version.
Under the heading Fact check, list each fact from your own list and mark it Kept, Changed or Missing in each version. Note anything the assistant added that wasn't in the draft.
Fix any problems, by follow-up prompts or by hand, and copy your final versions.

checks.text: The staff announcement has a subject line and keeps the key dates and place: RoomBook from 3 March, the spreadsheet read-only from 28 February, training on 27 February at 10:00 and 14:00 in Room 2.14, and bookings to check by 5 March.
The contact address is exactly right.
A team-chat version of no more than 50 words is included.
Every fact is checked in both versions, and anything changed, missing or added is noted.
The kitchen closure is left out, or the submission explains it should go in a separate message.

lab.submit: Paste your final staff announcement, your Chat version and your Fact check list.

files.content: hi all, so as some of you know were moving away from the old booking spreadsheet for meeting rooms (finally!!) and going to a new system called RoomBook, it starts 3 March and the old spreadsheet will be read only from 28 February so please dont add anything to it after that. you'll need to log in with your normal work account. theres training, two sessions, 27 February at 10:00 and 14:00 in Room 2.14, 30 mins each, no need to book just turn up. if you have bookings in the spreadsheet for after 3 March facilities will move them over for you but check them by 5 March and tell us if anythings wrong. questions to facilities@example.com. also the 4th floor kitchen is closed next week for repairs sorry. thanks, Sam

hints: Training is two 30-minute sessions with no booking needed: check the rewrite hasn't turned it into one session or asked people to book.
If the assistant adds a weekday to a date, check it: the draft gives no year, so a weekday may be wrong.

modules.title: Research and summarising, with checking
modules.summary: Summarise long documents for a purpose, research unfamiliar topics, and check claims against sources, so you can rely on what you pass on.

lessons.title: Summarising long documents
objectives: Ask for summaries shaped by their purpose and reader
Get summaries you can check against the source
key_points: Tell the assistant why you need the summary and who it's for, such as 'the five rules a new starter must know', because a summary for one purpose leaves out what another needs.
Ask for a structure you can check: key points with the section or page each came from, and exact quotes for anything critical.
Very long documents may not fit in what the assistant can take in at once; if a summary seems to skip later sections, split the document and summarise each part.
Summaries often drop exceptions and conditions, such as 'only with director approval', so check rules and limits against the source.
Ask the assistant to say when the document doesn't cover something, rather than letting it fill the gap from general knowledge.

walkthrough.title: Summarise with sources you can check

steps.do: Paste or upload a document and ask for a summary with its purpose, reader and references.
steps.code:
Summarise the document below for a new employee in their first week.
Give the 5 rules that matter most, each with the section it comes from.
Use only the document. If something a new employee would need isn't covered, say so instead of guessing.

Document:
"""
[paste the document here]
"""
steps.see: Five rules, each with a section number you can look up.

steps.do: Ask for the exact wording behind a rule you'll rely on.
steps.code: Quote the exact sentence from the document behind rule 3.

steps.do: Find the sentence in the document yourself and compare. If the quote isn't in the document word for word, treat the rule as unchecked.

lessons.title: Researching with an assistant
objectives: Use an assistant to get started on an unfamiliar topic
Tell the difference between an answer from training data and one from sources
key_points: An assistant is a good starting point for research: it can explain unfamiliar topics, suggest questions to ask, outline the arguments on each side and propose search terms.
Without web search or documents to work from, it answers from training data that may be out of date or wrong, and it can invent sources that look real.
When an assistant searches the web or reads documents, it can cite them; open the sources and check they exist and say what's claimed.
For decisions that matter, go to primary sources, such as the law itself, official statistics or the original study, rather than relying on a summary of them.
Ask for counter-arguments and limitations, which guards against a one-sided answer that simply agrees with how you framed the question.

lessons.title: Checking claims before you rely on them
objectives: Decide how much checking a claim needs
Check facts, figures and quotes efficiently
key_points: Check in proportion to the stakes: a brainstorm needs little checking, while a figure in a board paper or a statement to a customer needs a reliable source.
Numbers, dates, names, quotes and references are where errors most often hide, so check each one against the original.
Lateral reading means checking a claim by seeing what other independent, reliable sources say about it, rather than judging one source by how convincing it looks.
Asking the assistant how sure it is, or what would change its answer, can show weak spots, but its confidence isn't proof; only a source is.
Keep a note of which claims you've checked and where, so you, and anyone you share the work with, can see what's verified.

lab.title: Summarise and fact-check a policy
lab.goal: Summarise a fictional travel policy for new staff, check every rule in the summary against the policy, and see how the assistant handles a question the policy doesn't answer.
setup: A chat assistant such as Claude
Download travel_policy.txt: a fictional travel and expenses policy

steps.do: Ask for a summary of no more than 120 words for new staff, and a list of the six rules they're most likely to need, each with its section number. Tell it to use only the policy.
Check each of the six rules against the policy. Under the heading Checked rules, mark each one Correct or Wrong and give the section, quoting the policy's words for any that are wrong.
Ask a question the policy doesn't answer.
steps.code: Using only the policy, can I claim for a taxi to the airport?

steps.do: Note whether the assistant said the policy doesn't cover it or gave an answer anyway. Search the policy yourself to confirm.
Ask for a corrected summary if anything was wrong or missing, such as a condition or limit, then copy it under the heading Final summary.

checks.text: The summary keeps the key limits and deadlines right, including hotels at 110 a night outside capital cities, flights booked 14 days ahead and claims within 30 days.
Each of the six rules is marked Correct or Wrong with its section.
The taxi question is tested, and the submission says whether the assistant admitted the policy is silent on it (it is) or made an answer up.
A final summary corrects anything that was wrong or missing.

lab.submit: Paste the assistant's first summary and six rules, your Checked rules list, the taxi question with its answer and your note on it, and your Final summary.

files.content:
TRAVEL AND EXPENSES POLICY (a fictional sample for this course)

Section 1. Scope
This policy applies to all employees from 1 April. It replaces the previous travel guidelines.

Section 2. Booking travel
Book all flights and trains through the travel desk. Flights must be booked at least 14 days before departure unless your manager approves a later booking. Economy class is standard. For flights longer than 6 hours, premium economy is allowed with your director's written approval.

Section 3. Hotels
The nightly limit, including breakfast and taxes, is 150 in capital cities and 110 elsewhere. Book through the travel desk, or book yourself and claim the cost back if the travel desk cannot find a room within the limit.

Section 4. Meals
When travelling overnight you may claim up to 50 a day for meals. Alcohol is not reimbursed. Meals with clients are covered by the hospitality policy, not this one.

Section 5. Using your own car
Business mileage is paid at 0.30 per kilometre. Travel between home and your usual workplace is not business mileage.

Section 6. Claims
Submit claims within 30 days of the expense, with itemised receipts. Claims submitted later than 30 days need your director's approval, and claims older than 90 days will not be paid.

Section 7. Exceptions
Any exception to this policy must be approved in writing by your budget holder before the trip.

hints: Conditions are easy to lose: premium economy needs a flight over 6 hours and a director's written approval.
Late claims aren't simply refused: after 30 days they need a director's approval, and after 90 days they aren't paid.

modules.title: Spreadsheets, meetings and your prompt library
modules.summary: Get and test spreadsheet formulas, turn meetings into action lists and plans, and save the prompts that work as templates you can reuse.

lessons.title: Spreadsheet formulas and data with AI
objectives: Describe a spreadsheet so an assistant can write the right formula
Test a formula before trusting it
key_points: Describe your sheet to the assistant: the column letters and headings, the rows the data is in and the result you want; you rarely need to paste the data itself.
Say which program you use (Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc), because some functions, such as XLOOKUP, aren't available in every program or version.
Ask the assistant to explain each formula in plain words, so you understand what it does and can spot when it's wrong.
Test every formula on a case you can check by hand, such as a filter that shows the same rows, before trusting it on the whole sheet.
Assistants can also suggest how to clean data, such as trimming spaces, splitting columns or fixing dates, and which chart or pivot table would answer a question.

walkthrough.title: Get, explain and test a formula

steps.do: Describe the sheet and the result you want, without pasting the data.
steps.code:
I use Google Sheets. Columns: A date, B employee, C department, D category, E amount. The data is in rows 2 to 21.
Give me one formula for the total amount where the department is Sales and the category is Travel.

steps.do: Ask what each part does.
steps.code: Explain each part of that formula in plain words.

steps.do: Paste the formula into the sheet, then check it by hand: filter for Sales and Travel, and add up the rows you see.
If the results differ, tell the assistant what you expected and what you got, and ask what could cause the difference, such as extra spaces in the text or numbers stored as text.

lessons.title: Meetings and planning
objectives: Use an assistant to prepare agendas and turn notes into actions
Plan a project or a week with an assistant's help
key_points: Before a meeting, an assistant can turn a purpose and a list of topics into an agenda with timings and the decision needed on each item.
After a meeting, it can turn notes or a transcript into decisions, actions with owners and due dates, and open questions; check the result against what was actually agreed.
Recording or transcribing a meeting needs the participants' agreement, and your organisation's rules may limit which tools can be used and what can be recorded.
For planning, an assistant can break a project into tasks, suggest an order, estimate rough effort and flag risks, which you then adjust with your knowledge of the work.
A weekly planning routine works well: paste your tasks and deadlines, ask for a prioritised plan, then decide yourself what to drop, delegate or move.

walkthrough.title: From meeting notes to an action list

steps.do: Paste rough notes, with names you may share or replaced by roles, and ask for a structured summary.
steps.code:
Turn these meeting notes into: 1) decisions made, 2) a table of actions with owner and due date, 3) open questions. If an action has no owner or date in the notes, write 'not agreed' rather than guessing.

Notes:
"""
[paste your notes here]
"""
steps.see: A table of actions, with 'not agreed' where the notes don't say.

steps.do: Check every decision and action against your memory or the notes, and correct anything that wasn't agreed.
Ask for a short follow-up email to the attendees with the decisions and actions, then check it before sending.

lessons.title: Building a personal prompt library
objectives: Turn prompts that worked into reusable templates
Measure which templates save time
key_points: A prompt library is a collection of prompts that worked, saved as templates for tasks you do often, such as weekly reports, replies to common questions or meeting summaries.
Write templates with placeholders in square brackets, such as [AUDIENCE] and [KEY FACTS], so you only fill in what changes each time.
Keep the library somewhere quick to reach, such as a document, a notes app, or your assistant's saved instructions or project features where it has them.
Note for each prompt what it's for, what good output looks like and what to check, and improve the template when you find a better wording.
Time a task with and without its template a few times, including the checking, to see which prompts really save time and are worth sharing with your team.

walkthrough.title: Turn a prompt that worked into a template

steps.do: Find a prompt that gave a good result, and ask the assistant to turn it into a template.
steps.code:
Turn the prompt below into a reusable template. Replace the details that will change each time with placeholders in square brackets, such as [AUDIENCE] or [DEADLINE], and keep everything else.

Prompt:
"""
[paste the prompt that worked]
"""

steps.do: Save the template in your library with its name, what it's for, what good output looks like and what to check.
Next time the task comes up, fill in the placeholders, run it, and note how long the task took including checking.

lab.title: Get the formulas right with an assistant
lab.tool: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
lab.goal: Use a chat assistant to write formulas that answer five questions about a team's expense claims, and check every answer before trusting it.
setup: A spreadsheet program and a chat assistant such as Claude
Download team_expenses.csv, a fictional month of expense claims, and open it in your spreadsheet

steps.do: Look at the sheet: A date, B employee, C department, D category, E amount, with data in rows 2 to 21. Describe it to the assistant, naming your spreadsheet program, but don't paste the data.
Ask for formulas for four results, and put each in column H with its label in column G: Travel total, Sales travel total, Claims over 100 and Average meal claim (shown with two decimal places).
Check one result by hand: filter the sheet for department Sales and category Travel, and add up the rows you see.
Ask for a formula for F2, copied down, that shows Needs approval for any Meals claim over 50 and nothing otherwise, and a formula that counts the flags.
Ask the assistant to explain the SUMIFS formula in plain words, and copy its explanation.
If any formula gave an error or a surprising result, note what was wrong and how you fixed it.

checks.text: The Travel total is 769.60.
The Sales travel total is 488.40, and it was checked by hand.
Claims over 100 are counted correctly: 6.
The average meal claim is 46.99.
Three meal claims are flagged for approval: Ana's 64.20, Farah's 71.40 and Elif's 55.00.
The SUMIFS formula is explained in plain words.

lab.submit: Paste your labels, formulas and results from columns G and H, the flagged rows, the count of flags, and the assistant's explanation of SUMIFS.
hints: If a total looks too small, check whether some amounts were imported as text: they sit on the left of the cell instead of the right.
If your spreadsheet uses a comma as the decimal separator, it also uses semicolons between arguments: =SUMIF(D2:D21;"Travel";E2:E21).
Use the cell format, or ROUND(…, 2), to show the average with two decimal places.

project.title: Save an hour a week: your AI workflow
project.brief: Choose three tasks from your own work that you do at least once a week, such as writing updates, summarising documents, preparing or following up meetings, or working in spreadsheets. For each, design a workflow with a chat assistant: a tested prompt template, the checks the output always needs, and the data that must never go into it. Time each task with and without the assistant over at least two rounds, including the time spent checking, and collect your templates in a prompt library you could share with a colleague. Use only material you're allowed to share: replace names and confidential details with placeholders, and follow your organisation's AI policy, or the rules from this course if it has none.
deliverables: A prompt library of at least five templates with placeholders, each with its purpose, what good output looks like and what to check
For each of the three tasks: the workflow, a sample input with personal and confidential details removed, the assistant's output and your final version
A time log: minutes per task with and without the assistant, including checking, over at least two rounds
A note on privacy and policy: which tool you used, what kinds of data went in, and why that's allowed
A short reflection: which workflow saves most time, what you still do by hand, and why

rubric.name: Useful, reusable prompts
rubric.description: Templates give context, task, audience, format and constraints, use clear placeholders, and produce good first drafts for the tasks they're meant for.

rubric.name: Checking and accuracy
rubric.description: Each workflow has specific checks for facts, numbers and commitments, and the final versions show the checks were done and errors corrected.

rubric.name: Measured time savings
rubric.description: The time log covers each task with and without AI, includes checking time, and the conclusions follow from the numbers.

rubric.name: Privacy and policy
rubric.description: No personal or confidential data appears; the note names the tool and plan, and explains why each kind of data used is allowed.

rubric.name: Reflection
rubric.description: The reflection is honest about where AI helped, where it didn't, and what stays a human job.

project.submit: Paste your prompt library, the three workflows with their samples and final versions, your time log, your privacy and policy note and your reflection.
